schools.summary: Gill reports the Jewish identification of the messenger, keeps the repeated phrase emphatic, and meets the objection that Jehu owed loyalty to Ahab's house.

Henry explains why Elisha sent a younger man, treats the privacy of the anointing as a test of Jehu's confidence in his commission, presses both halves of the royal title, and fixes the controversy on persecution rather than idolatry.

Clarke renders the phrase as the servant of the prophet, makes the title a charge to restore the pure worship, and grounds the sentence in the law of blood for blood; Wesley sets the idolatry aside and makes the prophets' blood the whole quarrel.

Ellicott credits Rashi with the identification, answers Reuss on the substitution of this narrative for one about Elijah, and allows Jezebel's persecution as probable; Keil and Delitzsch fix the inner chamber and prefer Schmidt's reason for the order to flee.

debates.question: Why was the messenger told to flee at once?

sides.position: To prevent all further discussion and keep him from mixing in other affairs, not to guard him from Ahab's adherents
To avoid questioning and give the act greater force
To leave Jehu without a witness, so that his confidence in the commission would be its own proof

debates.question: Had Jehu been anointed privately once already?

sides.position: No; the supposition fails, since Hazael must then have been anointed privately too
The act discharged the commission given to Elijah, and Reuss's document theory is pure conjecture

outliers.note: Alone in answering a named critic at length, that Reuss's reconstruction is conjecture and his portrait of Elisha as a revolutionary whose name legitimised the new dynasty is being considerably wiser than our only authorities.

themes: gird up thy loins, and take this box of oil
I have anointed thee king over Israel
smite the house of Ahab thy master
the dogs shall eat Jezebel
1.pericope_label: Gird up thy loins: I have anointed thee king over Israel

schools.summary: Gill reconstructs what made the captains disbelieve Jehu's answer, and denies that the garments were wearing apparel at all.
Henry reads the captains' word as contempt for a life of self-denial, finds the same charge laid against Christ and Paul, and adds that Jehu did nothing without the captains' consent.
Clarke rebukes the officers for scoffing at a holy man, reports the Chaldee for their denial, and builds the sun-dial reading of the stairs; Wesley notes they knew him a prophet by habit and gesture.
Ellicott offers ridicule for one inspired, puts their alarm first, renders their denial as trickery, and draws out the trust it gave Jehu; Keil and Delitzsch settle the stairs on Kimchi's bare steps.

debates.question: What did Jehu mean by telling them they knew the man?

sides.position: A reproof: they knew him for a prophet and should not have called him mad
Agreement with their contempt, as a way of putting them off
A probe of their disposition, or a refusal to answer what they had already divined

debates.question: What is meant by the top of the stairs?

sides.position: The public sun-dial, built in steps, and probably the same one on which the sign was later given to Ahaz
The bare steps themselves, with Kimchi, the early translators having merely guessed

outliers.note: Alone in denying that the garments were the captains' own clothing, making them carpets or tapestry laid so that Jehu might sit raised and conspicuous.

themes: wherefore came this mad fellow to thee?
ye know the man, and his communication
it is false; tell us now
they put it under him on the top of the stairs
11.pericope_label: Wherefore came this mad fellow to thee? Jehu is king

schools.summary: Gill states the confederacy plainly and reads the chariot as state and majesty.
Henry measures the march from Ramoth-gilead to Jezreel and makes the whole of it expedition and precaution against the news outrunning Jehu.
Clarke supplies the campaign, the city taken and then watched because Hazael meant to retake it, and Joram gone to Jezreel to be cured.

Ellicott argues from the order that Ramoth was held and not besieged, against Josephus, and glosses the idiom of consent; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same military conclusion from the verb used of Joram.

debates.question: Was Ramoth-gilead held by Israel or besieged by them?

sides.position: Held: the order that no fugitive leave the city is unintelligible on a siege, whatever Josephus relates
Held: the verb used of Joram means defending the city against Hazael, not laying siege to it
State and majesty, Jehu riding as a king
Nothing but speed, the news not to outrun him

outliers.note: Alone in naming Josephus as the authority for a siege and in refuting him from the internal logic of Jehu's own command.

themes: Jehu conspired against Joram
Joram had kept Ramothgilead because of Hazael
if it be your minds, let none go forth
Jehu rode in a chariot and went to Jezreel
14.pericope_label: Jehu conspired against Joram and rode to Jezreel

schools.summary: Gill gives the watchman his ordinary duty and reads the king's question in its widest sense, of the army, the kingdom and the riders' intent.
Clarke makes the watchmen a national system of signal posts, and takes the furious driving as Jehu's established and almost proverbial character.

Ellicott fixes the tower by the palace, infers a considerable force from the word for the troop, denies that Joram was yet apprehensive, and reports the Targum and Josephus for the opposite sense of the driving; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the refusal and render the driving as a madman's.

debates.question: What was the force of the king's question to the riders?

sides.position: Whether all was well with the army or the kingdom, and whether they came as friends or enemies
No more than what is the news, Joram not yet apprehensive; against Thenius, who would have suspected a king to send more than one horseman
Furiously, as his campaigns had established and as the word for madness implies
Quietly and in order, on the reading of the Targum and Josephus, which Ellicott traces to a confusion of two similar words

outliers.note: Alone in treating the watchmen as an institution, a chain of posts within hearing of one another serving as a kind of telegraph for the whole country.

themes: there stood a watchman on the tower
is it peace?
what hast thou to do with peace? turn thee behind me
the driving is like the driving of Jehu
17.pericope_label: There stood a watchman on the tower: the driving of Jehu

schools.summary: Gill has Joram take the reins himself, and is careful that Bidkar was now Jehu's captain though he had served Ahab and his son.

Clarke takes the whoredoms literally and observes that Jehu could hardly have objected to the calf-worship, endorses the marginal reading of the bow, and argues that Naboth's sons must have died with him; Wesley allows both senses of the charge and calls the arrow one of God's.

Ellicott makes the kings' want of an escort proof they suspected nothing, takes the whoredoms spiritually, corrects Keil on the idiom of the bow, and lists the versions on how the two men had ridden behind Ahab; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the cry of treachery and the prophetic burden.

debates.question: Are the whoredoms charged on Jezebel literal or figurative?

sides.position: Literal, there being much reason to think she patronised an impure religion
Spiritual, that is, idolatries
Both at once, the literal and the figurative supporting each other

debates.question: What does the phrase about filling the hand with the bow mean?

sides.position: That Jehu took up the bow, set his arrow and let fly; the margin is correct
That he seized the bow
That he had already set an arrow on the bow, to fill a bow being to stretch it

outliers.note: Alone in noticing that Jehu's charge against Jezebel can hardly have included the calf-worship, to which Jehu was himself favourably disposed.

themes: they met him in the portion of Naboth
is it peace, Jehu?
what peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother
the arrow went out at his heart
21.pericope_label: Is it peace, Jehu? In the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite

schools.summary: Gill has the body carried to Jerusalem by Jehu's leave, granted for Jehoshaphat's sake, and reckons the regnal years as a co-regency.

Clarke sets out the discrepancy with the later history and quotes Lightfoot's harmony for it, and explains the regnal years by a viceroyalty during Joram's sickness; Wesley harmonises in a different order and holds that Chronicles was written to supply what Kings omits.

Ellicott reconstructs the pursuit and the ascent of Gur, prefers the Greek for the missing clause, counts the definite places a mark of trustworthiness, and rejects the attempt to combine the two accounts; Keil and Delitzsch read the wound as mortal but not immediate and supply the lost clause as a copyist's loss.
Lightfoot supplies the harmony at length, Ahaziah hiding in Samaria and being brought out to be slain towards Gur, with Kings short and Chronicles showing the order.

debates.question: How is this account of Ahaziah's death to be squared with the later one?

sides.position: By harmony: he hid in Samaria, was brought out and smitten towards Gur, and died at Megiddo
By harmony in another order: Megiddo first, then Samaria, capture, sentence and death at Megiddo
By neither: the places named here mark the better account, Rashi's and Keil's combination is revolting to common sense, and one text is probably corrupt

debates.question: Why do the regnal years differ between the accounts?

sides.position: A co-regency, the son reigning first with his father and then alone
Loose synchronism between the two kingdoms, and the verse may be a parenthesis and not original

outliers.note: Alone in refusing harmonisation outright, naming Rashi and Keil and calling their reconciliation revolting to common sense, and preferring to assume a corrupt text in one narrative or the other.

themes: Ahaziah fled by the way of the garden house
smite him also in the chariot
he fled to Megiddo, and died there
buried him in his sepulchre with his fathers
27.pericope_label: Ahaziah fled and died at Megiddo

schools.summary: Gill notes that the news reaching Jezebel included what Jehu had done to Joram.
Henry reads her conduct as three refusals, to hide, to humble herself and to tremble, tests the precedent of Zimri and finds it misapplied, and makes her fall a type of the ruin of persecutors.
Clarke gathers the practice of eye-painting from Persia, Rome and Barbary and passes on Jarchi's view of her motive; Wesley reduces her words to a reminder that Zimri's treason was briefly enjoyed.

Ellicott identifies the pigment, holds that she dressed to die a queen, and offers two accounts of her opening words; Keil and Delitzsch describe the paint and its application and say Jehu did not deign to answer her.

debates.question: Why did Jezebel paint and dress?

sides.position: To daunt Jehu and put him out of countenance
To disarm him and induce him to take her to wife, on Jarchi's view
To die a queen, in her royal apparel

debates.question: What did Jezebel's words to Jehu mean?

sides.position: A threat backed by a precedent, that a regicide enjoys his treason briefly
A conciliation, telling him that killing a master was nothing new, or else an ironical salutation to the slayer
A mocking inquiry after his health, with the question her son had thrice asked now put by the sovereign herself

outliers.note: Alone in testing the analogy she draws and rejecting it, Zimri having acted from his own ambition where Jehu was anointed by a son of the prophets and acted by order from heaven.

themes: she painted her face, and tired her head
looked out at a window
had Zimri peace, who slew his master?
an unhumbled heart under humbling providences
30.pericope_label: Jezebel painted her face: had Zimri peace, who slew his master?

schools.summary: Gill has Jehu look up on hearing her words and reads the order as throwing her from the window to the ground.

Clarke recoils at the manner of her death, passes on the rabbinical account of why the dogs left skull, feet and hands, and closes on how literally the prediction was fulfilled; Wesley notes that Jehu had forgotten the charge about the dogs and that he called her a king's daughter and not a king's wife.

Ellicott explains the eunuchs' readiness against Thenius, takes the singular verb of Jehu driving over the body, finds a touch of remorse in the burial order, and contradicts Keil twice on the closing oracle; Keil and Delitzsch report what was left and read the last verse as Jehu's free expansion of Elijah's words.

sides.position: The horses, as all the versions have it, excited by the blood according to Thenius
Jehu, in the sense that he drove over the fallen body; Ewald goes beyond the text in having him spurn her with his feet

debates.question: Is the last verse part of Elijah's prophecy?

sides.position: Yes, but freely expanded by Jehu, since it stands nowhere in those words
Yes, and probably original rather than any expansion, the earlier book's differing word being a simple loss of a letter

outliers.note: Alone in weighing what Jehu did not say, that he called Jezebel a king's daughter and not a king's wife, lest he seem to show any respect to the house of Ahab.

themes: who is on my side? who?
throw her down
they found no more of her than the skull
so that they shall not say, This is Jezebel
32.pericope_label: Throw her down: they found no more of her than the skull
